HEADLINE: How house prices will perform in 2017
TEXT:
It might not hit the boomtime peaks of 2013 but a survey of property analysts shows most are predicting solid growth in the price of houses in 2017.

It's a different story for apartments, and indeed for all property in "gloom-time" cities Perth and Darwin where analysts have consistently predicted more price falls.

But if you're in a house in Sydney or Melbourne, you can rest easy. After four strong years that saw prices in Sydney and Melbourne grow by 67 per cent and 46 per cent respectively, it seems we haven't reached the end of the run just yet, according to research house CoreLogic.

"We literally had our biggest week this year in numbers and value in mid December," said buyer's agent Simon Cohen of Sydney firm Cohen Handler.

"I think the market will remain pretty strong."

But if you have properties in Perth or Darwin or even Adelaide, the prognosis is not positive. In mining regions, CoreLogic's head of research Tim Lawless said there was no sign of them climbing out of a hole.

With the Holden production line due to close next year, Adelaide's economy remained weak with few Australians choosing to move there, BIS Shrapnel Residential Property senior manager Angie Zigomanis said. "There's more downside there than upside."

But in between the two extreme ends of the property spectrum lie some surprising nuggets of opportunities - Canberra and Hobart.

"Like the eastern seaboard versus Western Australia, there is the property market of Hobart versus the rest of Tasmania. There's something about Hobart that's attracting people there and the main demographic is not retirees," Mr Zigomanis said. "It's the people who are winding down."

The strong Sydney and Melbourne markets have allowed these wealthy Australians to cash out of their properties and buy in seachange cities such as Hobart, much like what happened in the last boom of 2000, he said.

Likewise Canberra is expected to roar into action after a return in government employment and a steadier economy following the federal election in July.

Unlike the last few years, the headline buyers in all markets next year are likely to be local - investors, owner-occupiers or first home buyers - with fewer foreign buyers, analysts say.

Forecasts for national capital city price growth range from 1 to 12 per cent. Top of the prediction league table is property research group SQM Research's call of a national price growth of between 8 and 12 per cent, assuming the Reserve Bank of Australia cuts the cash rate by 0.25 percentage points in the middle of 2017.

If that happens, SQM said Sydney prices might leap by as much as 18 per cent, followed closely by Melbourne at 17 per cent. If the cash rate remains unchanged in 2017, prices will still rise between 6 and 10 per cent.

"Affluent areas tend to be driven by the prosperity of local economy. And right now, both Sydney and Melbourne have the fastest growing economies in the nation," SQM managing director Louis Christopher said. BIS Shrapnel and CoreLogic's forecasts were more conservative. CoreLogic's Mr Lawless said the outlook for 2017 was "becoming increasingly challenging to give direction on".

"On one hand we have dwelling values broadly rising across most capital cities, however, as we look below the surface, it is clear that individual housing markets are at very different stages of the cycle and responding to vastly different economic and demographic conditions," he said.

"The smaller capital cities, where the pace of capital gains has been trending higher, are likely to see a continuation in these trends as investors start to look more favourably at markets with a higher yield profile that are also earlier in the growth cycle."

Mr Lawless expects Sydney and Melbourne prices to grow between 9 and 10 per cent next year while Perth and Darwin will continue to lose value.

BIS Shrapnel has forecast a low 1 to 3 per cent house price growth across the national markets, mainly held back by falling apartment prices in Brisbane, Melbourne and parts of Sydney. For houses, BIS Shrapnel said prices would rise in all capital cities except Perth and Darwin. Sydney and Melbourne will top the chart at 4 per cent.

AMP Capital Chief Economist Shane Oliver remains bearish on apartments.

In the next two years, Dr Oliver has reaffirmed his prediction Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane apartment prices will fall as much as 15 to 20 per cent because of the "massive multi-dwelling building boom".

While Melbourne and Brisbane apartment prices will fall evenly throughout the city, Dr Oliver said Sydney would have pockets of price falls in Parramatta, inner west Sydney and Bankstown. "There's a [supply] indigestion problem but Sydney won't have a supply problem for another two years," he said.

Including houses, he thinks national capital city price gains will slow to about 3 to 4 per cent.

Property Investment Professionals of Australia chairman Ben Kingsley said with borrowing rates edging up and negative gearing still a political target, investors faced uncertain times.

"But there are still plenty of opportunities to be found for investors ... the long-term fundamentals of well-selected property remain strong."

On the other hand, rising prices spell more bad news for housing affordability.

"All levels of government need to take responsibility, which is why we need a deal between the Commonwealth, states and territories to incentivise reform to fix housing supply," Property Council chief executive Ken Morrison said.

Sydney

In Sydney, first-home buyers and local investors will continue to fossick in growth suburbs, while wealthy Baby Boomers, mainly in the form of downsizers and empty nesters, will flood the boutique and inner-city suburbs in 2017, Colliers International NSW Residential director David Chittenden said.

The appetite for apartments will be replaced by one for houses and middle housing such as townhouses, Mr Chittenden added.

"In 2017, we expect to see greater demand for terrace and town home product, in the wake of ever-reducing land lot sizes, coupled with the desire to live as close as possible (affordable) to commercial amenity.

"High-quality master planned projects in primary locations should also perform well, such as Randwick."

Hobart, Canberra

The are good prospects for Canberra and Hobart, both Corelogic's Mr Lawless and BIS Shrapnel's Mr Zigomanis agreed.

"The smaller capital cities, where the pace of capital gains has been trending higher, are likely to see a continuation in these trends as investors start to look more favourably at markets with a higher yield profile that are also earlier in the growth cycle," Mr Lawless said.

Hobart may be attracting wealthy east coast property buyers but Canberra is attracting returning government workers.

"Canberra is strong in terms of construction and its public sector return and the spillover from Sydney [property buyers] will continue to 2017, [from 2016]," BIS Shrapnel associate director Kim Hawtrey said.

Dr Oliver said Canberra and Hobart are likely to get about a 3 to 4 per cent increase in house prices.

Adelaide

Analysts had little to contribute to the Adelaide outlook except to say its house prices will merely go "sideways".

In SQM Research Mr Christopher Boom and Bust report, he wrote: "There just isn't much happening in the housing market. There are no rises. There are no falls. It's just flat for both the sale market and the rental market."

Perth, Darwin

Analysts and most investors hold the view that prices in Perth still have some way to go downwards. The problem in Perth has also been exacerbated by too much supply against a falling population. The Reserve Bank said Perth property developers failed to respond to the dwindling population, triggered by the mining downturn.

Darwin's issue lies in its soft economy and rising unemployment. But Mr Christopher is of the view Darwin could well be close to the bottom.

Melbourne

Melbourne could well surpass Sydney as the growth city, some non-traditional punters have said.

Tabcorp's online website Luxbet, which is taking bets on which capital city will take the gong for the biggest capital appreciation for 2017, is paying the highest odds for Melbourne at $3.

Corelogic index already shows Melbourne catching up to Sydney with the year on year price increase at 13.39 per cent. Sydney prices have risen 14.53 per cent.

But the one to look out for in Melbourne is apartments. BIS Shrapnel said apartment median prices could fall by up to 3.5 per cent in 2017.

Brisbane

Brisbane's housing market remains the most controversial.

JLL's latest research says a large supply of apartments in the Brisbane market over the next two to three years, coupled with below average population growth, will have short-term impacts.

"Capital growth is expected to be limited in the short to medium term, and we could see downward pressure on rents," JLL head of residential research Carol Hodgson said.

The Real Estate Institute Queensland September-quarter results show falling median prices as a result of the apartment supply, but say with possible job growth from employers such as the Adani Carmichael coal mine, price falls could be mitigated.

"Jobs mean growth and the regional communities of Townsville, Mackay and Rockhampton have been declared as hubs for the Adani workforce, which is great news for those real estate markets," REIQ chief executive Antonia Mercorella said.

HEADLINE: How economics is changing dating game
TEXT:
Data and real-life dating the equation to improve the matchmaking odds.

What do economic theories such as the Nash equilibrium and the optimal stopping problem have to do with finding love? The answer may help explain why single men and women are turning their backs on internet matchmaking services in favour of face-to-face dating events.

That doesn't mean online dating is dead but, as Louise O'Connor and husband Brett Couston have found, combining the power of computers to crunch data with old-school face-to-face meetings is helping with the medium's one big problem: the gross inequality of attention.

"Often on online sites, you will get a handful of people inundated with hundreds and hundreds of messages whereas the vast majority of people won't get as many," says O'Connor, whose Cityswoon hybrid online and speed-dating business is trying to make the best of both worlds.

"Because you have to match everyone in the room, we use an algorithm to measure their compatibility and match people with the highest compatibility score."

The problem is neatly illustrated in the film A Beautiful Mind in which mathematician John Nash uses the Nash equilibrium theory to explain the optimal outcome for everyone is to target less attractive women in the group.

"If we all go for the blonde, we block each other, not a single one of us is going to get her so then we go for her friends," he explains. "But they will all give us the cold shoulder because no one likes to be the second choice.

"What if no one goes for the blonde? We don't get in each other's way and we don't insult the other girls. That's the only way we all get laid."

This theory partly explains the popularity of face-to-face matching services such as Cityswoon when dating opportunities on free apps such as Tinder and Bumble abound.

Until September, the company was hosting about four speed-dating events a month. Now it hosts 20 a month in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Canberra and Perth.

Before the event, participants are asked a number of standard questions, such as height and education, and others, including: "Have you ever taken dance lessons?", "Wouldn't it be fun to chuck it all in and sail around the world for a year?", "If you found out your partner was lying to you, how would you react?" and "Are your parents still together?".

They are matched based on their answers and have 10 to 15-minute "dates" with six to eight people.

Shadow assistant treasurer and author of The Economics of Just About Everything Andrew Leigh says, in principle, online dating brings together people who would never have found one another.

But, in reality, online daters can run into the optimal stopping problem because of the perceived ease of meeting new people on these platforms.

The optimal stopping problem refers to the decision paralysis people face because they never know how their current opportunity compares with all the other opportunities that may come up in the future.

"Anyone who tried to sell a car or a house is familiar with this," Leigh says. "You can keep it on the market, hoping you will find the perfect buyer, or you can settle. In practice, it is better to settle than to hold out forever. The same is true in online dating."

He says online dating can lead people to search endlessly for love in the hope of finding the perfect person rather than meeting someone with whom they can build a future.

"There is a risk with online dating that it fools people into thinking that love is panning for gold rather than building a house," he says.

"The risk there is people fall into the mistake of thinking true love is mining rather than manufacturing. In my experience, true love is not about finding someone who has a set of trades and doing nothing.

"True love is about finding somebody who you have a great affinity with and working really hard to build a shared connection over the course of the lifetime."

O'Connor says the optimal stopping problem can be exacerbated on online dating platforms because it is easy to dismiss people on the basis of objective criteria - that is, they're not as hot as they could be - in the hope of finding the best partner.

But in real life, people tend to make decisions based on chemistry and connections rather than a set of checklists, she says.

"Online dating is almost like looking through a catalogue. In person it's really different because you can meet a man who has got everything on paper but there's no spark when you meet him. Or you may have a connection with someone even though they have less of what you're looking for."

misa.han@fairfaxmedia.com.au

HEADLINE: Bitcoin surges 17pc in a week
TEXT:
Chinese and Indian investors hoping to evade strict capital controls and circumnavigate cash restrictions have flooded into Bitcoin, sending the cryptocurrency soaring 17 per cent in one week and topping off a dramatic year for the volatile asset class.

The price of Bitcoin - the encrypted currency underpinned by blockchain technology - shot through a key resistance level at $US800 at the end of last week, and has continued to soar higher, peaking at $US911 ($1268) before settling around $US900 on Tuesday, close to a three-year high.

"We are seeing a wave of Indian buyers looking to circumnavigate the recent push to remove large slabs of cash from circulation and who otherwise have trouble moving fiat currency," said Sam Lee, chief executive of Blockchain Global, formally Bitcoin Group and developer of Australia's largest bitcoin exchange.

"That, combined with Chinese traders who are using Bitcoin as a natural hedge to the devaluation of the yuan, is driving the Bitcoin price to these highs."

Bitcoin reached a record of $US1216.73 on the Mt Gox exchange in November 2013, a result of frenzied market speculation, but has traded within a band of $US450 and $US600 for most of 2016.

Investors evading capital controls in mainland China, a persistent reduction in yuan exposure and an interest in speculation and gambling generally underpin the cryptocurrency's often violent movements, but broader market dynamics have also played a large part in the price volatility, say traders.

In the lead-up to the Brexit vote in June, Bitcoin climbed 47 per cent, acting as it does in the face of market uncertainty as a "safe-haven" asset class.

"Bitcoin is an uncorrelated asset class and a valuable hedging mechanism," said Joe Lee, founder of leveraged Bitcoin trading platform Magnr, at the time. "In an investor portfolio where there is macroeconomic uncertainty fuelled by local politics, diversifying outside of the geographical boundary becomes imperative."

HEADLINE: Tailored luxury: it's expensive, but priceless
TEXT:
The boutique experience goes beyond the hotel room walls.

It's been a while since a comfortable bed and a good shower added up to a luxurious hotel stay.

But as tourists flood into Australia in ever-growing numbers, several new hotel property openings illustrate just how far hoteliers are going to ensure their seasoned travellers check out with memories of experiences.

And it's not before time. Leisure travellers are driving much of the rapid growth in visitor arrivals into Australia - a total of 8.14 million people arrived for the year ending October 2016, an increase of 11.5 per cent on last year - and many will be comparing our boutique hotels with those in more developed markets around the world.

Tracy Atherton, general manager of soon to open Jackalope Hotel on Victoria's Mornington Peninsula, says Australian hotels are finally, slowly, catching on to the authentic boutique experience by thinking outside just the hotel room walls.

"My job at Jackalope is to create a memory, not just a hotel room," Atherton says. "Mainstream Australian hotels have been very slow to catch on. I worked with Aman Resorts for 10 years, and they nailed that concept. Travellers today are after an experience, a story."

The 46-room Jackalope is scheduled to open next April and considering it will be the region's most expensive luxury hotel (from $650 per night), Atherton is already finalising those defining drawcard experiences.

"The hotel is set on a working vineyard, so we will offer things like private breakfast in the middle of the vineyard, barrel tastings, private tours with winemaker Geraldine McFaul, candlelit turndown, reserving poolside chairs," she says.

"We will offer a package where we find out your favourite drink before you come and stay with us, for example a Negroni, that would be mine, and for the duration of the stay, that drink will be on us, wherever you order it on the property."

While she admits the room rates aren't cheap - with the property development already creeping upwards of $40 million, including the land purchase three years ago - she says if they do their job right, the lasting memory will be not of the bill but of the experience.

Atherton was most recently general manager of Hotel Hotel in Canberra and admits that boutique property was also a game changer.

"When we opened Hotel Hotel three years ago, it was a changing point for the hotel industry in Australia," she says. "There are lots of boutique city hotels around the world, in London, Berlin, New York, but at the time there was nothing really in Australia."

She sees Jackalope as changing the landscape on a similar scale. "We are merging hospitality and art on a deeper level, with bespoke artworks, sculptures, light installations all part of the property's unique site narrative."

Site-specific narrative is also the starting point for every QT Hotel, including the newly opened QT Melbourne. David Seargeant, managing director of Event Hospitality and Entertainment, says the aim of the new property was to capture the spirit of Melbourne, so even a 188-room hotel felt intimate.

"With every hotel, we create a guest experience that's relevant and tailored to the destination," he says. "We captured the essence of Melbourne with multi-layered design, a lot of detail, with reference to the early rag trade with an industrial feel of raw concrete and black metal."

"We are at the Paris end of Collins Street too, so we have a lot of black and white French styling and an incredible pastry shop."

The staff can't be cookie cutter, either. QT Melbourne features stylishly dressed directors of chaos greeting guests at the entrance, the mini-bar and gift store has Melbourne-centric items, no two guest rooms are the same and the public spaces, such as the rooftop bar and restaurants, help immerse a guest into the city's food and wine scene immediately.

HEADLINE: Slaters' $250m class action just got harder
TEXT:
Maurice Blackburn will likely have to widen the net of a class action against Slater & Gordon to include its former auditors after the corporate regulator reopened an investigation into the embattled law firm's accounts.

Slater & Gordon revealed last week that Australian Securities and Investments Commission has asked for documents that may show whether the law firm's financial records were "deliberately falsified or manipulated", or whether its "officers have committed offences".

This is critical to Maurice Blackburn's case because if it is proved that Slater's executives engaged in "falsification", insurers would not be liable for any class action claim. Instead, Maurice Blackburn would have to go after other sources, including its auditors, advisers and directors personally.

Maurice Blackburn said in a statement last week: "Slater & Gordon's announcement does indicate that the ASIC investigation is very serious, and we will be watching with interest.

"But in complex class actions like this there are often multiple avenues of recovery, especially considering that Slater & Gordon itself has foreshadowed a cross-claim against other parties, including a warranty claim against Quindell (now Watchstone) and £50 million ($85 million) is still being held in escrow against that claim."

Slaters is planning to sue Watchstone Group - the remnants of British company Quindell - which it paid $1.3 billion in a deal to acquire its troubled professional services division. The stock is trading at 23¢ compared to a high of $7.85 18 months ago.

A senior litigation lawyer, who did not wish to be named, said if allegations of falsification are proven, Maurice Blackburn has three options: for the law firm to "stick to the knitting" and allege failure of continous disclosure obligations without raising allegations of falsified accounts; to go after the directors individually; or to seek to recover from third parties including auditors and advisers.

Another senior litigation lawyer said if the corporate regulator finds there has been deliberate falsification of accounts then it is likely Maurice Blackburn would go after third parties including Slater's auditors. Slater's former auditors include Pitcher Partners and EY.

"If you have a falsification of accounts and that's done willingly, then insurance exclusions could kick in, which means you have an uninsured loss and have got to find other sources to recover the money from," he said.

"It's much more likely they will also go after somebody who was insured, for example a negligent adviser who was a concurrent wrongdoer. In practice it'll be the accountants who signed off on the accounts, because in theory it's their job to discover things like [falsification]," he said.

In October Maurice Blackburn launched a $250 million plus class action on behalf of more than 3000 shareholders, including over 80 institutional investors and super funds. The size of the class action is significantly more than Slater & Gordon's market cap of just $81.9 million.

The action is backed by litigation funder International Litigation Partners.

Diane Jones, executive of JustKapital, a litigation funder which is conditionally funding ACA Lawyers' planned class action against Slater, said any claim of falsified accounts is a "significant concern" for any litigation funder because it would render insurance ineffective.

But she said it was likely the ACA class action will proceed even if there is an ASIC investigation under way.

Another litigation lawyer said, while the investigation will trigger Maurice Blackburn and other class action litigators to "widen the net" to ensure recoverability, it was unlikely they would go after the personal wealth of the individual directors because "none of them would have the independent wealth to meet a judgment".

misa.han@fairfaxmedia.com.au

jonathan.shapiro@fairfaxmedia.com.au

Key points

Class action may need to be widened to include former auditors.

The class action size is more than S&G's market cap.

HEADLINE: LITTLE PEOPLE, BIG DATA ADD UP
TEXT:
Social infrastructure is a lucrative gap in the market, writes Nick Lenaghan.

What started as a cottage industry is now embracing artificial intelligence, as childcare centres owners harness the predictive power of big data to forecast supply and demand.

Put simply, while their little tenants are tripping through their ABCs, childcare landlords are firing up complex algorithms to divine where next to invest in development.

Artificial intelligence is revolutionising stockmarkets and high finance. It might also provide the means to marshal multiple levels of information needed to forecast where childcare demand will become most acute.

The $430 million Arena REIT and the $630 million Folkestone Education Trust represent the next generation of property trusts.

Traditionally, real estate investment trusts have focused on office towers, shopping centres and sprawling logistics facilities.

That thesis is changing as investors, institutional and retail, chase higher yields and governments and not-for-profit players become less willing to hold property.

A new class of real estate is emerging: social infrastructure, the property that sits behind sectors such as childcare, healthcare and student accommodation.

With a background in the data-rich environment of retail property, Arena REIT managing director Bryce Mitchelson is applying the lessons of demography to childcare. In the end, he says, it's all about market share.

The trove of information collected at Arena has expanded rapidly. Mitchelson and his team track every one of the 6767 childcare centres in Australia.

That tally is accompanied by increasingly dense information about population growth, income levels, participation rates and development pipelines, as well data about the size and quality of each facility.

"The level of data that we can now source … it's gone beyond the old days of having a gut feel of 'this feels under-supplied in this area let's do something'," says Mitchelson.

"Now you can actually analyse it out with all the data and prove up whether it is under-supplied or not."

The ratio of children to childcare places is 3.63 nationally, but it varies greatly from suburb to suburb. In Melbourne's inner west, around Seddon and Kingsville, the ratio rises to 25:1. "If you put a centre there you'll have kids falling out of the trees trying to get in," Mitchelson says.

In Sydney, where it can be harder to get hold of land, the ratio in Forestville is 20:1 and 16:1 in Hunters Hill.

But it would be a mistake to simply build on the current snapshots. Weighing the factors determining demand with a wealth of information, Mitchelson has turned to data analytics. That high-powered number crunching can uncover correlations and identify relationships that are not yet understood by childcare landlords, he says. "The algorithm will come back and tell you: you should be building here. There is a lot more certainty around the investment case."

About 98 per cent of the capitalisation of Australia's key REIT index is accounted for by office, retail and industrial property.

Outside the top 200 property stocks, 39 per cent of the capitalisation in real estate is due to non-traditional assets, including social infrastructure.

In the US, just 53 per cent of REIT capital is held in traditional assets. "There is clear evidence that our REIT sector is morphing towards the non-core sectors," says Petra Capital analyst Jonathan Kriska.

Even so, there is an old-style property story underlying the new asset class.

Office towers values fell about 20 per cent and shopping centres dropped 15 per cent in the wake of the financial crisis. In contrast healthcare property slipped just 5 per cent. Childcare dipped 10 per cent.

The listed landlords typically strike so-called triple-net leases on long terms, making childcare tenants responsible for much of the property costs.

SMSF investors have also come into the sector, in search of better yields than those of a typical high street retail property.

Their interest has helped drive around 300 basis points in yield compression in the past two to three years, according to Kriska.

The squeeze on yields is evident at the regular Burgess Rawson auctions, where childcare centres are hot property.

In April, a Chatswood facility on Sydney's North Shore sold for $2.41 million on a record low yield of 3.9 per cent.

Childcare centres at Burgess Rawson auctions now regularly trade on yields below 5 per cent. In regional areas centres they sell on yields of 6 per cent to 6.75 per cent. "People are pulling their money out of the bank and buying assets around $2 million to $3 million. There's always a lot of interest in those assets," says Burgess Rawson's Natalie Couper.

The appetite in the direct market is being felt at Folkestone and Arena, which revalued their portfolios, tightening cap rates further and pushing values up by 9 per cent. It adds to the case for developing new facilities rather than buying existing centres. And it's why Mitchelson is chasing algorithms. "Investment is all about looking forward," he says. "If you can find an under-supplied spot which will be so in five years' time and you put supply in earlier you can capture that market."

HEADLINE: DELIVERING THE REAL EXPERIENCE
TEXT:
Chinese visitor numbers have soared in recent years and a new breed of wealthy traveller could see numbers surge further. But is Australia ready to take full advantage? Michael Smith reports.

Jack Lee and 11 of his friends are in search of fresh air, fresh seafood and a decent Pinot.

This group of Hong Kong-based Chinese professionals spent Christmas in Melbourne before flying to Tasmania on Boxing Day. They did not come to Australia to shop at Louis Vuitton or follow a flag-waving tour guide around the Sydney Opera House. Instead, they have been drawn here for its wide-open spaces, sunshine, and the farms and vineyards of the Mornington Peninsula and the Tamar Valley.

"The Australian cuisine, weather and the space is what is really attractive for me. People now are looking for these qualities, a real experience, rather than just shopping," Lee, 38, says in an interview from the luxurious South Yarra house his group rented before flying to Launceston.

"Tasmania's nature really attracts me. I want to visit the farms, vineyards, markets etc. Hopefully I can see some the Aurora ... the Southern Lights, too."

Lee, who works for a French fashion company, does not fit the cliche image of the Chinese tourist. He lives in Hong Kong, whose residents have traditionally had more sophisticated tastes than their mainland counterparts. But this is rapidly changing.

The large groups are still pouring out of coaches on the Great Ocean Road or under the Sydney Harbour Bridge. But they are rapidly being superseded by this new breed of young, professional, and bilingual visitor that Australian tourism authorities say are the key to the biggest economic windfall Australia's stagnant economy can hope for at the moment.

But they are also demanding. They want good hotels, free Wi-Fi, efficient service and fantastic food. "The type of Chinese consumer coming is really changing They are much smaller groups, two to four, and they are looking for experiences like self-drive and are really interested in the food culture of the country and the produce as well," Tourism Australia managing director John O'Sullivan tells AFR Weekend, noting 65 per cent of visas are now issued to individual travellers instead of groups.

"We are still focused on targeting this independent traveller that has a high disposable income and is more inclined to seek out higher-end experiences, repeat visitation and the smaller group size because we know that is where the yields will come from."

There is a lot of hype around the influx of Chinese visitors into Australia at the moment. Tourism Minister Steve Ciobo says tourism grew at more than three times the rest of the economy in the 2015-16 financial year. Chinese tourists spend about $8000 per trip compared with an average of $5000 by other international visitors.

The number of Chinese visitors has jumped 20 per cent over the past year to 1.1 million in 2016. They will keep on climbing to at least 1.3 million in 2017 before hitting 3 million within a decade, according to IBISWorld analysis. More direct aviation routes are opening up and Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull and Chinese Premier Li Keqiang have designated 2017 as the "Australia-China Year of Tourism".

China may drive the biggest tourism boom in Australia since the Japanese flocked here in the '80s but one senior official says to achieve that "we need quality at every level".

Australia's natural scenery and fresh food are prime attractions but several industry players interviewed for this article warn Australia is expensive, and offers inferior service, compared to places such as Asia. Europe is increasingly seen as unsafe but Australia must try harder if it wants to compete with Rome's history or Paris' shopping.

Despite the impressive growth Australia still only commands 1 per cent of the 120 million Chinese tourists globally in 2015, well below rates in New Zealand, Thailand and Japan, according to global tourism data. The Australia China Relations Institute says Australia's share of outbound tourism actually fell from 1.2 per cent in 2000 to 0.8 per cent now.

Others are worried that the country's infrastructure would not cope if Australia doubled its share of the Chinese market to 2 per cent.

"We have discussed that disproportion in meetings with FIRB (Foreign Investment Review Board). We say ... well 1 [per cent] could become 2 easily ... and there are pale faces in the room because they know our infrastructure couldn't handle that kind of uptick in tourism overnight," says one senior executive.

While the biggest hotel construction boom in decades is under way, big Chinese tour operators say there are not enough reasonably priced rooms in Sydney and Melbourne to keep up with demand.

"The biggest problem is the hotels, especially in Sydney and Melbourne. Sometimes the price is very expensive. If events like the Australian Open or Formula One are on, the price can increase from $180 to $500 a night," says Kevin Xu, the general manager of Melbourne-based Grand City Travel Group, one of the bigger agencies catering to Chinese tourists.

Xu says more Australians working in hospitality speak Mandarin is a positive, but notes Chinese tourists complain it still takes too long to process visas or claim tax refunds at airports. He says many visitors book their trip at the last minute but then find they cannot get their visa processed in time.

"If they don't have the visa they don't buy the ticket and if they don't have the ticket we can't book anything for them. By the time they get the visa the hotel price has increased. This market is very hard," Xu says.

Tourism Australia and the federal government have not been sitting on their hands, however, when it comes to the China tourism opportunity. Key policy changes include the introduction of a 10-year multiple entry visa for Chinese tourists and an important "open skies" agreement signed in early December, giving Chinese airlines unrestricted access to the Australian market.

O'Sullivan admits it is challenging keeping up with such a fast-growing market and one of Tourism Australia's priorities in 2017 would be to change the way it "talks" to Chinese consumers, who are early adapters of technology. Only 14 per cent of Chinese tourists booked trips on mobile phones in 2014 but this jumped to 54 per cent in 2015.

"With a market like China, because it is so big and so fast moving, you are never in absolute terms 100 per cent ready. To say you are 'China ready' today and you don't have to do anything between now and 2020 is nonsensical. You need to continually evolve and adapt with this market and any of our markets.

"We will more aggressively develop our social media and pay footprint in China."

Tourism Australia has a goal of 20,000 new hotel rooms by 2020 as part of its 10-year strategy and has been working with Austrade to target Chinese investors such as the Wanda Group which is building a new luxury hotel in Sydney. There are more high-end hotels under construction in Australia than there have been in decades. New boutique hotels are springing up in Adelaide, on Sydney's Bondi beach and casino giants Crown Resorts and The Star have major projects under way in Sydney and Brisbane.

Virgin Australia chief executive John Borghetti, who is partnering with China's HNA Group to launch flights to the region this year, says China is a large and complex market and it is important for Australian businesses to have a strategy to harness that. "We also have to be smart about the other elements for growth in this market," he says. "This is why we're planning to form an alliance with HNA Group to work together in other areas like distribution and travel promotion. I think we rate fairly well in the region in terms of quality of tourist infrastructure, but there is always room for improvement, particularly when it comes to promoting Australia's advantages to international travellers."

Airlines and retailers are racing to capitalise on the China story. Qantas, which starts flying direct to Beijing on January 25, publishes a Chinese-language version of its in-flight magazine which is popular with advertisers seeking to reach premium customers, and is recruiting more cabin crew who can speak Chinese.

"While Chinese travel demand is likely to remain strong, the challenge is making sure Australia remains on the 'go to' list for the travellers themselves. It's about making Chinese visitors feel welcome," Qantas chief Alan Joyce said in Chanticleer's annual CEO survey.

Myer CEO Richard Umbers says his flagship stores have bilingual staff, sell products popular with Chinese shoppers and will have special promotions during Chinese New Year in January.

"In these stores, we have appointed bilingual team members, identifiable by national flag icons on their name badges, and bilingual concierge services, to provide advice and assistance to shoppers. In addition, since last year, all Myer stores now offer China UnionPay, as a payment type, making it easier for Chinese tourists to purchase products using their preferred card," he told The Australian Financial Review.

China Southern Airlines president Tan Wangeng, who was in Australia in December for the airline's inaugural Guangzhou-Adelaide service, said he expected 20 per cent annual growth in Chinese tourism numbers to continue for another few years. But he and other Chinese airline executives are concerned about congestion and the curfew at Sydney Airport. They are concerned a second airport for the city at Badgery's Creek is still a decade away.

Gavin Norris, the president of Australia and New Zealand for online real estate portal Juwai.com, is surprised that Australia's share of the Chinese tourism market lags well behind the number of Chinese buying property or studying Down Under.

"There is a yawning gap between the way the typical Chinese customer of ours looking at real estate sees Australia's competitiveness versus tourism," says Norris. Juwai.com, the biggest property portal Chinese consumers use to buy property overseas, says Australia accounts for around 30 per cent of global real estate traffic for the Chinese market, second to the United States, which has 45 per cent. This compares to just over 1 per cent of the Chinese tourism market.

"We have a place of beauty here rather than anything of any historical significance, you have to be bilingual when you come here and despite the FX movements we are still fairly costly compared to our competitors," Norris says. "Maybe that is why we have a small share."

Juwai.com was founded by two Australians and plans to float on the Australian Securities Exchange in 2017.

Tourism operators also point to the enormous opportunity for regional Australia as Chinese visitors board direct flights to cities like Adelaide or venture out of the big cities for wilderness and wildlife experiences.

"Before just the rich or the businessmen would travel. Now more and more people from the smaller cities in China are coming here. They like different things. They like the scenery in Australia," Xu says. Many are more interested in outdoor activities like shooting, golf, diving and even skydiving. He has booked large VIP groups wanting to go to Hamilton Island and Hayman Island.

Direct flights to Adelaide, for example, are expected to bring more visitors to the Barossa Valley and the Flinders Ranges. A new aquarium in Cairns and the Field of Light event at Uluru are also expected to lure more Chinese tourists.

Chinese New Year, which falls in late January this year, will be one of the busiest times for Australian tourism operators. There is no doubt the economic opportunity is there but the trick will be ensuring those visitors want to come back a second time.

HEADLINE: Woolworths to sell petrol network to BP for $1.8b
TEXT:
Woolworths will sell its petrol station portfolio to BP in a $1.8 billion deal that will help the retail giant fund its ongoing fight to regain market share in the grocery sector.

It is understood the deal was signed over Christmas and ended the two parties' months of negotiations around price, loyalty agreements, fuel discount vouchers and their respective convenience strategies.

Under the terms of the deal, BP will get 500 Woolworths-branded fuel and convenience outlets.

It is understood BP will pay $1.8 billion cash and other benefits to Woolworths. The funds are expected to shore up Woolworths' balance sheet and help fund chief executive Brad Banducci's supermarkets strategy.

Woolworths did not comment on Tuesday.

The deal is expected to be announced on Wednesday (December 28) - the first day of trading on the share market since Christmas.

The Woolworths network sells about 4 billion litres of fuel a year and had earnings of around $130 million to $150 million.

The deal is expected to create one of the country's largest fuel and convenience retailer networks, level-pegging with the ASX-listed Caltex.

Under the deal, which was foreshadowed by the Street Talk column, it is expected Woolworths "Metro" brand will be retained across the network and Woolworths will continue to supply the stores.

This will allow Mr Banducci to continue with the retailer's push into the important convenience market, where it has aimed its small-format Metro stores, and will see the grocer continue to offer its 4¢ a litre discount vouchers.

BP has experience with this model. In 2004 it partnered with British retail icon Marks & Spencer and has now rolled out almost 250 petrol station stores under the Simply Food brand. Under that deal, BP operates the stores and takes an undisclosed share of profits.

This week the head of BP's downstream business, Tufan Erginbilgic, said the company was looking to replicate the strategy outside Britain; it has a deal in Germany and said it was in talks with three other retailers around the world. "It is a global strategy," Mr Erginbilgic told The Telegraph of London. "The more we roll out, the more differentiated our offer will be - and earnings will obviously grow."

The deal will require the approval of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission. ACCC chairman Rod Sims made it clear that the deal is firmly on his radar. The Australian petrol sector is dominated by Caltex Australia and Viva Energy, which operates the Shell brand; the pair have nearly half of the market.

It is understood that BP is preparing to argue that the tie-up would make BP a similar size to Caltex. The deal is expected to take about 12 months to complete.

BP edged out Caltex Australia in the race for the Woolworths network. In a move that appeared to pre-empt the Woolworths decision, Caltex announced on December 22 that it had paid $324 million for fuel distributor Gull New Zealand in a deal that will see it grab 5 per cent of the Kiwi market, including a fuel import terminal in the North Island and 77 retail outlets.

Morgan Stanley ran the auction for Woolworths.

HEADLINE: Tapping the talent pool of stay-at-home mums
TEXT:
A new online marketplace is offering high-level, part-time jobs for mums to combat the "false promise" of flexibility offered by the gig economy.

Beam, which is in its pilot stage and will have its official launch early next year, intends to tap into the hidden workforce of stay-at-home parents by offering them work during school hours, with jobs starting at 9.30am and ending at 2.30pm.

Its founders, Victoria Stuart and Stephanie Reuss, who previously worked at Google and business advisory giant Corporate Executive Board, said they started the company after becoming parents themselves and seeing how difficult it was for women to maintain leadership positions after having children.

Ms Stuart said degree-qualified mothers had become accustomed to the idea of taking on freelance gigs or low-skilled administrative jobs while they raised their children. However, they ignored the fact "so many lateral-thinking small to medium enterprises would do anything to attract that talent" and were willing to offer flexible hours to invest in the long term.

"Look at the whole talent pool of amazing women who dropped out of the workforce and who have a wealth of knowledge that remains untapped," Ms Stuart said.

"We said let's prevent that from going to waste and think about how to mobilise those people to get back into the workforce."

Beam is working with SMEs, including ticketing firm Eventbrite and female hygiene start-up TOM Organic, to offer parents high-level management and executives positions in temporary and part-time arrangements.

Private sector initiative and NSW government-backed "Jobs for NSW" provided Ms Stuart and Ms Reuss with a $5845 grant to scale and grow the online marketplace. The fund aims to invest in gazelles - companies that start small and grow rapidly - to fuel jobs growth. Beam arrives as the gig economy has undergone a dramatic expansion in Australia in recent months, with mothers now using smartphone apps such as Airtasker to do odd jobs while their children are at day care.

However, Ms Reuss said Beam aimed to fill in the gaps left by gig work, including job security and high-skilled work.

"The gig economy is a bit of a false promise for flexibility - what employees really want is an organisation that provides flexibility and work-life balance but also provides a deeper connection to the purpose of what they're doing and financial stability as well."

She said apps such as Uber "might be a big thing now but those transactional jobs are going to be automated so where does that leave the gig economy?

"What we believe is that while people are opting into this gig economy it may not be sustainable for them because they've got no other choice, no other destination to go for other flexible roles."
